claim: Fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) are documented to be present on alcohol-containing food sources.
source: For decades, numerous researchers have documented the presence of the fruit fly or Drosophila melanogaster on alcohol-containing food sources.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature documenting this phenomenon over decades.

claim: There is relatively little understood about the ethological relationship between flies and ethanol.
source: Although fruit flies are a common laboratory model organism of choice, there is relatively little understood about the ethological relationship between flies and ethanol.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Male flies become more aggressive when they inhabit ethanol-containing food substrates.
source: In this study, we find that when male flies inhabit ethanol-containing food substrates they become more aggressive.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The odor of ethanol potentiates the activity of sensory neurons in response to an aggression-promoting pheromone.
source: The odor of ethanol potentiates the activity of sensory neurons in response to an aggression-promoting pheromone.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data presented in the study.

claim: The odor of ethanol promotes attraction to a food-related citrus odor.
source: Finally, we observed that the odor of ethanol also promotes attraction to a food-related citrus odor.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data presented in the study.

claim: Aggression in Drosophila melanogaster is a well-documented behavior.
source: Aggression in Drosophila melanogaster is a well-documented behavior; studies have identified several aggression-regulating pheromones, circuits, and genes (Wang and Anderson, 2010; Vrontou et al., 2006; Nilsen et al., 2004; Asahina et al., 2014; Dow and von Schilcher, 1975).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: 11-cis-Vaccenyl acetate (cVa) is produced by males.
source: The most well-studied pheromone, 11-cis-Vaccenyl acetate (cVa) is produced by males and has been shown to increase aggression in male flies (Wang and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: 11-cis-Vaccenyl acetate (cVa) has been shown to increase aggression in male flies.
source: The most well-studied pheromone, 11-cis-Vaccenyl acetate (cVa) is produced by males and has been shown to increase aggression in male flies (Wang and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Most studies of cVa use this pheromone in isolation by adding it to a behavioral arena or painting flies with it.
source: Most studies of cVa use this pheromone in isolation by adding it to a behavioral arena or painting flies with it.
evidence: Statement about common experimental practices in the field.

claim: In the wild, flies will encounter cVa when they aggregate on fermenting fruits where they will experience cVa in combination with volatile compounds produced by fermentation.
source: However, in the wild, flies will encounter cVa when they aggregate on fermenting fruits where they will experience cVa in combination with volatile compounds produced by fermentation (Zhu et al., 2003; Keesey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on fly ecology.

claim: Little is understood about how ethologically relevant combinations of odors influence the underlying neurobiology of behavior.
source: Despite the ecological complexity of the fruit fly niche, little is understood about how ethologically relevant combinations of odors influence the underlying neurobiology of behavior.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ethanol is one of the products of fermentation.
source: Ethanol is one of the products of fermentation and fruit flies in particular are attracted to alcohol-containing fruits (<7% ethanol by volume) (McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about fermentation.

claim: Fruit flies are attracted to alcohol-containing fruits (<7% ethanol by volume).
source: Ethanol is one of the products of fermentation and fruit flies in particular are attracted to alcohol-containing fruits (<7% ethanol by volume) (McKenzie and McKechnie, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is no identified canonical ethanol olfactory receptor despite the fact that a wide range of ethanol-related behaviors have been identified in flies.
source: Remarkably, there is no identified canonical ethanol olfactory receptor despite the fact that a wide range of ethanol-related behaviors have been identified in flies (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Kim et al., 1998 identified an odorant-binding protein known as LUSH that mediates aversion to high concentrations of alcohol.
source: Kim et al., 1998 identified an odorant-binding protein known as LUSH that mediates aversion to high concentrations of alcohol.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: LUSH was the first protein shown to directly bind ethanol.
source: LUSH was the first protein shown to directly bind ethanol (Kruse et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the fly antennae, the only neurons known to respond to cVa are also those that express LUSH.
source: In the fly antennae, the only neurons known to respond to cVa are also those that express LUSH (Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: cVa-responsive neurons do not show any electrophysiological responses to ethanol alone.
source: However, these neurons do not show any electrophysiological responses to ethanol alone (Figure 1a and Kim et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1a and citation to prior research.

claim: Neither the 5% nor the 10% ethanol-containing foods caused any detectable rise in ethanol in the flies.
source: Neither the 5% nor the 10% ethanol-containing foods caused any detectable rise in ethanol in the flies.
evidence: Supported by hemolymph ethanol concentration measurements presented in the study.

claim: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in time spent fighting.
source: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in time spent fighting, number of fights they engaged in, and number of lunges executed (Figure 1c,d and e).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in number of fights they engaged in.
source: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in time spent fighting, number of fights they engaged in, and number of lunges executed (Figure 1c,d and e).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in number of lunges executed.
source: Males that fought on 5% ethanol-containing food exhibited an increase in time spent fighting, number of fights they engaged in, and number of lunges executed (Figure 1c,d and e).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Males on 10% ethanol food exhibited an increase in the proportion that lunged.
source: Although, males on 10% ethanol food exhibited an increase in the proportion that lunged and decreased latency to lunge, they did not show an increase in total number of lunges executed compared to control animals (Figure 1e,f & g).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Males on 10% ethanol food exhibited decreased latency to lunge.
source: Although, males on 10% ethanol food exhibited an increase in the proportion that lunged and decreased latency to lunge, they did not show an increase in total number of lunges executed compared to control animals (Figure 1e,f & g).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1f and g.

claim: Males on 10% ethanol food did not show an increase in total number of lunges executed compared to control animals.
source: Although, males on 10% ethanol food exhibited an increase in the proportion that lunged and decreased latency to lunge, they did not show an increase in total number of lunges executed compared to control animals (Figure 1e,f & g).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: When flies occupy food patches with ethologically relevant concentrations of ethanol, they display elevated levels of aggression that are not due to increased locomotion.
source: These data demonstrate that when flies occupy food patches with ethologically relevant concentrations of ethanol, they display elevated levels of aggression that are not due to increased locomotion (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data and locomotion measurements shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Males respond to cVa in a dose-dependent manner with low concentrations of cVa promoting aggregation and aggression, whereas high concentrations of cVa cause dispersion.
source: One possible explanation for the reduction of aggression in flies that fought on 20% ethanol compared to those on 5% ethanol can be explained by Wang and Anderson, 2010 observation that males respond to cVa in a dose-dependent manner with low concentrations of cVa promoting aggregation and aggression, whereas high concentrations of cVa cause dispersion (Wang and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Twenty-percent ethanol may have potentiated the cVa signal so that it mimics a high cVa concentration causing males to disperse and spend less time fighting.
source: Twenty-percent ethanol may have potentiated the cVa signal so that it mimics a high cVa concentration causing males to disperse and spend less time fighting.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Ethanol does not acutely activate cVa-responsive neurons.
source: Although ethanol does not acutely activate these neurons, we found that it substantially enhanced their cVa responses (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ethanol substantially enhanced cVa responses in cVa-responsive neurons.
source: Although ethanol does not acutely activate these neurons, we found that it substantially enhanced their cVa responses (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: 30% ethanol substantially increased cVa-evoked activity (Δ Spikes).
source: We found that 30% ethanol substantially increased cVa-evoked activity (Δ Spikes), while 5% ethanol increased activity to a lesser extent (Figure 2c,e,f and g).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: 5% ethanol increased cVa-evoked activity to a lesser extent than 30% ethanol.
source: We found that 30% ethanol substantially increased cVa-evoked activity (Δ Spikes), while 5% ethanol increased activity to a lesser extent (Figure 2c,e,f and g).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: T1 neurons have an unstimulated spontaneous firing rate of approximately 1 Hz.
source: These T1 neurons have an unstimulated spontaneous firing rate of approximately 1 Hz and increase their firing in response to cVa (Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: T1 neurons increase their firing in response to cVa.
source: These T1 neurons have an unstimulated spontaneous firing rate of approximately 1 Hz and increase their firing in response to cVa (Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Spontaneous responses consistently increased when 5% or 30% ethanol was applied.
source: Spontaneous responses consistently increased when we applied 5% or 30% ethanol (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The time constant to deactivation increased with 30% ethanol application indicating that neurons had greater sustained activity following cVa treatment.
source: Finally, the time constant to deactivation increased with 30% ethanol application indicating that neurons had greater sustained activity following cVa treatment (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The electrophysiological data are consistent with the notion that ethanol increases inter-male aggression by potentiating responses to cVa.
source: These data are consistent with the notion that ethanol increases inter-male aggression by potentiating responses to cVa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: In the wild, ethanol is almost always present with other fruit volatiles and fermentation odorants.
source: In the wild, ethanol is almost always present with other fruit volatiles and fermentation odorants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the natural environment of flies.

claim: Farnesol is an odorant present in the rinds of citrus fruits, which are known to be attractive to flies.
source: Farnesol is an odorant present in the rinds of citrus fruits, which are known to be attractive to flies (Ronderos et al., 2014; Dweck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Or83c neurons are not broadly tuned and display strong activation to farnesol.
source: We chose farnesol because Or83c neurons are not broadly tuned and display strong activation to farnesol (similar to how cVa-sensing neurons are only tuned to cVa) and do not show a response to ethanol alone (Ronderos et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Or83c neurons do not show a response to ethanol alone.
source: We chose farnesol because Or83c neurons are not broadly tuned and display strong activation to farnesol (similar to how cVa-sensing neurons are only tuned to cVa) and do not show a response to ethanol alone (Ronderos et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Both evoked activity and spontaneous activity of ai2 sensilla increased following ethanol treatment.
source: We found that both evoked activity and spontaneous activity increased following ethanol treatment (Figure 3b-e).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3b-e.

claim: A 10−5 dilution of farnesol elicited no attraction when used alone.
source: We used a dilution of farnesol that elicited no attraction when used alone (10−5).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data presented in the study.

claim: When combined with 30% ethanol the odor from a 10−5 dilution of farnesol displayed much greater attractiveness than either the odor of farnesol or ethanol alone.
source: However, when combined with 30% ethanol the odor from a 10−5 dilution of farnesol displayed much greater attractiveness than either the odor of farnesol or ethanol alone (Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Flies preferred the mixed farnesol and ethanol odor over farnesol alone or ethanol alone suggesting ethanol potentiates attraction to farnesol.
source: Flies preferred the mixed farnesol and ethanol odor over farnesol alone or ethanol alone suggesting ethanol potentiates attraction to farnesol.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral assay data.

claim: Previous studies on behavioral responses of Drosophila to ethanol have focused on the systemic effects of ethanol.
source: Previous studies on behavioral responses of Drosophila to ethanol have focused on the systemic effects of ethanol.
evidence: Statement about prior research focus in the field.

claim: Flies become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol.
source: These studies demonstrated that flies, like mammals, become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol, sedate at high doses of ethanol, acquire tolerance to ethanol, display a withdrawal response, and seek ethanol despite negative consequence (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Flies sedate at high doses of ethanol.
source: These studies demonstrated that flies, like mammals, become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol, sedate at high doses of ethanol, acquire tolerance to ethanol, display a withdrawal response, and seek ethanol despite negative consequence (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Flies acquire tolerance to ethanol.
source: These studies demonstrated that flies, like mammals, become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol, sedate at high doses of ethanol, acquire tolerance to ethanol, display a withdrawal response, and seek ethanol despite negative consequence (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Flies display a withdrawal response to ethanol.
source: These studies demonstrated that flies, like mammals, become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol, sedate at high doses of ethanol, acquire tolerance to ethanol, display a withdrawal response, and seek ethanol despite negative consequence (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Flies seek ethanol despite negative consequence.
source: These studies demonstrated that flies, like mammals, become hyperactive with low doses of ethanol, sedate at high doses of ethanol, acquire tolerance to ethanol, display a withdrawal response, and seek ethanol despite negative consequence (reviewed in Park et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Ethanol responses described in this paper are most likely olfactory (non-systemic) and are ethologically important to the life of a fly.
source: However, ethanol responses described in this paper are fundamentally distinct in that they are most likely olfactory (non-systemic) and are ethologically important to the life of a fly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing olfactory potentiation without systemic ethanol absorption.

claim: Fischer et al., 2017 demonstrated that flies are more attracted to natural mixtures of microbial by-products than the individual components of the mixture.
source: Fischer et al., 2017 demonstrated that flies are more attracted to natural mixtures of microbial by-products than the individual components of the mixture.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ethanol potentiates two fundamentally distinct odorants and behaviors in Drosophila.
source: We find evidence that ethanol potentiates two fundamentally distinct odorants and behaviors in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental data on cVa and farnesol.

claim: Ethanol odor increases cVa signaling, which in turn increases aggression.
source: First, ethanol odor increases cVa signaling, which in turn increases aggression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Ethanol augments farnesol signaling, resulting in increased attraction to this food odorant.
source: Second, ethanol augments farnesol signaling, resulting in increased attraction to this food odorant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Female flies are thought to prefer to consume ethanol-laden food because ethanol has caloric value, antimicrobial properties, and provides a protected niche by suppressing competition from other Drosophila species that find the ethanol to be toxic.
source: Female flies are thought to prefer to consume ethanol-laden food and lay their eggs in ethanol-containing food because ethanol has caloric value, antimicrobial properties, and provides a protected niche by suppressing competition from other Drosophila species that find the ethanol to be toxic (Kacsoh et al., 2013; Park et al., 2018; Azanchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Female flies are thought to prefer to lay their eggs in ethanol-containing food because ethanol has caloric value, antimicrobial properties, and provides a protected niche by suppressing competition from other Drosophila species that find the ethanol to be toxic.
source: Female flies are thought to prefer to consume ethanol-laden food and lay their eggs in ethanol-containing food because ethanol has caloric value, antimicrobial properties, and provides a protected niche by suppressing competition from other Drosophila species that find the ethanol to be toxic (Kacsoh et al., 2013; Park et al., 2018; Azanchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When female flies accumulate on the food substrate, males eventually follow, and fight one another for a chance to mate with the female.
source: When female flies accumulate on the food substrate, males eventually follow, and fight one another for a chance to mate with the female.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly mating behavior.

claim: Male flies are known to deposit cVa directly onto food substrates.
source: Interestingly, male flies are known to deposit cVa directly onto food substrates and will spend more time around the marked area (Keesey et al., 2016; Mercier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Male flies will spend more time around areas marked with cVa.
source: Interestingly, male flies are known to deposit cVa directly onto food substrates and will spend more time around the marked area (Keesey et al., 2016; Mercier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both the cVa pheromone and farnesol odorant are naturally encountered by flies in the wild and evoke behaviors believed to provide selective advantages.
source: Both the cVa pheromone and farnesol odorant are naturally encountered by flies in the wild and evoke behaviors believed to provide selective advantages.
evidence: This combines established knowledge with inference about evolutionary advantages.

claim: The odor of ethanol combined with a food odor could enhance the perceived value of the food as a reproductive resource.
source: The odor of ethanol combined with a food odor could enhance the perceived value of the food as a reproductive resource, while the combination of the scent of ethanol and cVA could increase the male drive to fight for control of this resource.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The combination of the scent of ethanol and cVA could increase the male drive to fight for control of this resource.
source: The odor of ethanol combined with a food odor could enhance the perceived value of the food as a reproductive resource, while the combination of the scent of ethanol and cVA could increase the male drive to fight for control of this resource.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: It seems likely that ethanol could increase attraction to other food odors and perhaps other fly pheromones as well.
source: We documented evidence for potentiated responses to two odors, but it seems likely that ethanol could increase attraction to other food odors and perhaps other fly pheromones as well.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings with two odorants.

claim: Aggression chambers were assembled based on description by Mundiyanapurath et al., 2006.
source: Aggression chambers were assembled based on description by Mundiyanapurath et al., 2006. using a fly vial cut one inch high and glued to one petri dish.
evidence: This describes the methodology used, citing prior work.

claim: Single Sensillum extracellular electrophysiology was conducted according to de Bruyne et al., 1999.
source: Single Sensillum extracellular electrophysiology was conducted according to de Bruyne et al., 1999 using 3–5 days old w1118 flies.
evidence: This describes the methodology used, citing prior work.

claim: 1% cVa was used because the responses it evokes is most functionally relevant, as the magnitude of response it evokes is similar to exposing a virgin female to a male fly.
source: We used 1% cVa because the responses it evokes is most functionally relevant, as the magnitude of response it evokes is similar to exposing a virgin female to a male fly.
evidence: This is a methodological justification based on functional relevance.

claim: Data analysis was performed as reported by Xu et al., 2005.
source: Data analysis was performed as reported by Xu et al., 2005.
evidence: This describes the methodology used, citing prior work.

claim: One possible explanation for why we did not observe an increase in Δ Spikes with cVa and 5% ethanol even though 5% ethanol increased aggression is because the duration of exposure was considerably shorter (1 min) compared to the behavioral assay (30 min), which may not have allowed for sufficient accumulation of alcohol.
source: One possible explanation for why we did not observe an increase in Δ Spikes with cVa and 5% ethanol even though 5% ethanol increased aggression is because the duration of exposure was considerably shorter (1 min) compared to the behavioral assay (30 min), which may not have allowed for sufficient accumulation of alcohol.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for an apparent discrepancy in the data.

claim: Olfactory Traps were based on the protocol developed by Woodard et al., 1989.
source: Olfactory Traps were based on the protocol developed by Woodard et al., 1989 and were constructed using a 1.5-microfuge tube with a hole drilled on the cap.
